title: What Did Ancient Humans Do at Night?
want: to understand what the dark hours were for (and, unknowingly, to sleep the way your body was built to)
central_question: So what did they actually do for all those dark hours? (0:30)
stakes: A whole state of consciousness, lost without anyone noticing; your 2 a.m. waking gets misdiagnosed as a disorder.
obstacle: A wrong belief (modern sleep is 'normal'), reinforced by translators and by artificial light.

beats.text: Tonight you'll flip a light switch without thinking.
For 99.9% of history there was no switch; half of every life was spent in darkness.
Central question: what filled all those hours?
Start with fire: before it, moving at night meant being eaten.
Fire drew a 30-ft circle of safety, and it also added 2-4 usable hours a day.
A researcher's campfire study: day talk is work, night talk is mostly stories, so culture is born at the fire.
The night held something else: you were not designed to sleep the way you do.
A historian finds 500+ records of 'first sleep' and 'second sleep' with a waking gap.
Historians mistranslated it for centuries because they couldn't imagine it.
A 1992 darkness experiment makes volunteers fall into the same split pattern, with a meditative hormone state.
What killed it? Light: street lamps, gas, Edison.
Aside: 'curfew' means cover-fire; being out at night was suspicious or illegal.
We 'conquered' night and called it progress, and blue light now wrecks melatonin.
We erased a whole phase of consciousness; what if your insomnia is your body remembering?
Recap of the ancestral night, then back to the light switch.

loops.q: What did they do in the dark?
What did fire give beyond safety?
What else was happening at night?
What did people do while awake mid-night?
Is it real biology or just history?

turns: 0:05 the switch didn't exist for 99.9% of history
2:53 you were not designed to sleep like this
4:24 experts misread the evidence for centuries
ending: Closes on a calm recap of the ancestral night, then calls back to the opening switch: we traded all of it for that switch and never noticed.
facts: Q: what happened at night? A: a researcher's numbers that day talk was work and night talk was mostly stories.
Q: is split sleep real or folklore? A: a modern lab removes artificial light and volunteers fall into the split pattern within weeks.
jokes: Very few (~0.7/min). Each sits at the end of a story beat ('overnight, literally' on the fire beat; 'Daytime talk was work.'). No digressions.
template: Tonight you [ordinary modern act]. BUT for 99.9% of history [it didn't exist]. SO what did [ancestors] do instead? First, [enabling thing]; it gave them [hidden gift] -> [named researcher's finding]. BUT there was more: you weren't built to [modern habit]. [Old records] showed it; experts missed it because [wrong belief]. THEREFORE [modern experiment] proves it's still in you. SO what killed it? [modern invention]. BUT here's what we lost: [X]. What if your [modern 'problem'] is your body remembering? Close: we traded it for [the opening object].

title: The Calhoun Effect
engine: real-person discovery (experiment chronicle with a myth-correction twist)
protagonist: John Calhoun and his eight founder mice
want: Calhoun wants a final answer to 'what happens to a society when nothing is hard?'
central_question: Everything was perfect, yet five years later all were dead with no diagnosable cause; what killed them? (0:10)
stakes: The colony dies out, and by extension the warning applies to us.
obstacle: An invisible cause (no scarcity, no disease) plus a popular misreading of the result.

beats.text: Eight mice in a perfect world: unlimited food and water, no threats.
Five years later every one is dead, and no vet could name a cause.
Meet Calhoun: he built a 'paradise' to test life when nothing is hard.
He had already seen the same collapse 24 times; #25 was meant to be the definitive run.
The setup: built for about 3,800 mice, which it 'would never come close to'.
Day by day: 104 calm days, then doubling, 600+ by day 315.
Normally surplus mice emigrate, and here there was nowhere to go.
Young males with no role sink into listless piles.
A second group turns frantic and hypersexual; females retreat to the top.
Mothers can't defend nests, abandon or eat their young; the social fabric is dead.
The survivors' kids become 'the beautiful ones': perfect fur, no social life.
Peak 2,200 on day 560, last conception day 920, last mouse dies 1973.
The world read it as 'comfort kills'.
Calhoun's own words say the killer was the loss of meaningful roles.
And Calhoun wasn't a doomer: he spent his career looking for the fix.
Callback to the opening; the mice had no choice, we still do.

loops.q: What happens to a society when nothing is hard?
How many will it reach (never near 3,800)?
Where do the surplus mice go?
What behaviours no mouse society had seen?
How will the next generation behave?
Is 'comfort kills' what he really said?

turns: 0:10 a paradise ends in total extinction
6:37 the famous lesson is a misreading
ending: Repeats the cold-open facts (eight mice, five years, an unnameable cause) and hands the stakes to the viewer: they had no choice, we do.
facts: Q: why does crowding break this colony? A: normal colonies shed surplus mice by emigration, and this one had no exit.
Q: what killed them? A: Calhoun's own sentence about roles outnumbered by individuals.
jokes: Almost none (~0.35/min). Irony only from names ('walk-up apartments', 'beautiful ones'). The story carries it.
template: [N subjects] were placed in a perfect [world]. [Time] later, all [failed], with no obvious cause. [Named person] built it to answer [big question]; he'd seen it [N] times, and this was the final test. Timeline: [calm phase] -> [growth] -> BUT [missing escape valve] -> THEREFORE [symptom 1] -> BUT [symptom 2] -> [darkest symptom] -> [a generation that looks perfect but is dead] -> [end date]. Everyone concluded [popular myth]. BUT his paper actually said [real cause]. AND he spent his life trying to [fix]. Callback to the opening; [they] had no choice, you do.

title: Why You Can't Remember Being a Baby
want: to recover/understand the first three years of your own life
central_question: You lived a whole life before age 3 and remember none of it; why, if 'brain not ready' is wrong? (0:10-0:20)
stakes: Your identity: is the baby in your photos even you?
obstacle: A wrong belief (babies can't record) and the brain's own growth.

beats.text: You lived a full life before age three: first word, first steps.
You remember none of it.
The usual answer, 'brain not ready', is wrong: something destroyed the memories.
Freud named it; a ribbon-and-mobile experiment proves babies do remember for days and weeks.
Those memories never reach adulthood, and for decades nobody knew why.
Layer 1: the hippocampus isn't wired yet.
That's only half; in 2014 two neuroscientists propose building the brain erases memory.
Mouse experiments confirm it: not too weak, too busy growing.
Another layer: no sense of self yet (mirror-and-rouge test).
An uncomfortable question: is the baby in your photos actually you?
One more piece: language gives memory a skeleton.
Culture shifts the age of first memory (2.5 to 4+).
Recap: everything at once.
Reframe: your brain was busy becoming you, which meant destroying who came before.

loops.q: Can building a brain really erase it?

turns: 3:03 not too weak, too busy growing
4:25 baby-you may be a different person
6:29 forgetting was the price of becoming you
ending: Explicit recap of all layers, then a philosophical sting: becoming you required destroying the person before.
facts: Q: can babies form memories at all? A: the ribbon-kick experiment (yes, for days or weeks).
Q: what destroys them? A: the neurogenesis study, where speeding new neurons makes adult mice forget.
jokes: Near zero. Tension comes from repeated 'even stranger' escalations.
template: You [did/experienced X] and remember none of it. Most people think [simple answer]. BUT that's not quite right: [stronger claim]. Proof the capacity exists: [experiment]. BUT [it vanishes]. Layer 1 [structural cause]. BUT that's only half: Layer 2 [counterintuitive cause, the thing that builds you destroys it]. Layer 3 [identity] -> uncomfortable question. Layer 4 [culture shifts it]. SO it was all at once. Close: [the loss] was the price of [becoming you].

title: What Did Ancient Humans Actually Eat?
central_question: Your fridge isn't food to them; so what did they actually eat? 'The answer would horrify you.' (0:08)
stakes: Survival then; now, a 3-million-year program misfiring in a world of donuts.
obstacle: Nature (scarcity, predators) and, today, our own outdated cravings.

beats.text: Open your fridge: soda, yogurt, pizza.
To your ancestors none of this is food; what did they eat? (proof is in caves)
3 million years ago we were scavengers: marrow from bones hyenas couldn't break, brains.
That's why your body still treats fat like treasure.
'What came later is worse': fire turns cooking into pre-digestion, guts shrink, brains grow.
The menu explodes; honey is about 15% of Hadza calories.
Same craving in you: modern sugar is honey in a costume.
Meat: one mammoth buys time for culture, and protein cravings follow.
One craving we can't admit: each other (cut-marked skull cups in an English cave).
It wasn't starvation: calorie math shows a human is poor food, so it was ritual.
Stranger still: they ate rotten meat on purpose, and cheese/beer are 'controlled rot'.
Every craving still runs; at 11 p.m. at the fridge you're running ancient code.
Role swap: you'd die in their world, and they'd think your kitchen is a god's pantry.
You may be the first human who isn't hungry.

ending: Callback to the opening fridge (now at 11 p.m.), a two-way time-travel swap, and a gratitude sting.
facts: Q: why do you crave fat? A: marrow and brains were the jackpot no other scavenger could reach.
Q: was cannibalism about hunger? A: calorie comparison of a human body vs a bison vs a mammoth.
jokes: ~1/min, placed at the end of each era beat as a modern translation ('sugar wearing a costume', 'controlled rot'). Each one bridges the beat back to 'you'.
template: Open your [modern thing]. To [ancestors], none of it is [category]. SO what did they [do]? (warn: horrifying). Era 1: [grim fact] -> 'your body still remembers' [modern craving]. BUT it gets worse. Era 2: [enabling tech] -> [body change]. Each era ends with a craving you still have ([modern product] = [ancient thing] in disguise). BUT one [thing] we can't admit: [taboo]. Not because [obvious reason]: [number that kills it]. AND stranger: [gross fact] -> [beloved thing is just that]. Close: [you at 11 p.m.] running ancient code; swap test both ways; you're the first who [doesn't suffer X].

title: What If WE Are The Aliens?
engine: versus/conflict (trial of a what-if hypothesis: case for, case against, residual mystery)
want: to know where we come from and why we don't fit
central_question: What if we don't fit on Earth because we're not from here? (0:22)
obstacle: Rival explanation (evolutionary mismatch) plus the honest limits of science.

beats.text: Every species is adapted to Earth: gills, hollow bones, fur.
We burn in our own sun, our spines fail, birth kills us.
Central question: what if we're not from here?
Exhibit 1: sunburn (we invented sunscreen against our own star).
Exhibit 2: 80% get back pain; we were 'retrofitted, badly'.
Exhibit 3: deadliest childbirth, most helpless babies.
Exhibit 4: allergies, our defences attack the air.
The strangest exhibit isn't physical: we alone know we'll die.
The hardest one: we dismantle our ecosystem like an invasive species.
Where from, then? The DNA co-discoverer proposed directed panspermia.
Supporting evidence: life appeared fast, meteorite amino acids, tardigrades survive space, a book arguing it.
Mainstream biology answers almost all of it: evolutionary mismatch, item by item.
'Settles it, right? Not quite': nothing explains our speed.
Candidate causes (language, cooking, FOXP2, teaching): none complete.
Honest verdict: probably not aliens, but we don't fully know.
Maybe the restlessness is a clue; either/or close.

loops.q: Which one is hardest to explain?
So where did we come from?

ending: Two-branch close: if we're from here we're the strangest thing Earth made; if not, we've been trying to get home without knowing. It ends on a question.
facts: Q: why do we burn? (later) A: hair loss for sweat-cooling on the savanna, the price of out-running everything.
Q: is the alien idea crank talk? A: a Nobel laureate co-wrote the 1973 paper.
jokes: Highest in the set (~1.9/min), but stacked on the 'case for' exhibits (0:28-3:53) as roasts of the species. The final 2 minutes are joke-free.
template: Every [peer] fits [environment]. Then there's [subject]: [3 misfits]. What if [wild hypothesis]? Case FOR: exhibit 1..5, escalating to 'the strangest one' and 'the hardest one'. SO a credible [authority] proposed [hypothesis] + supporting evidence. BUT mainstream [field] explains each exhibit (re-walk the list in the same order). 'Settles it, right? Not quite': [one residual anomaly]. Candidate explanations, none complete. Honest verdict: probably not, but not certain. Close on an either/or that makes the viewer feel strange and special.

title: Why Hasn't Anyone Raised the Titanic?
engine: mission/quest (obstacle ladder: 'why hasn't anyone done X?')
protagonist: would-be salvagers ('you', engineers, a salvage company)
want: to bring the Titanic back up
central_question: We know exactly where it is; why hasn't anyone just brought it up? (0:07)
stakes: A fortune and history, versus disturbing 1,500 graves; and the wreck will soon be gone either way.
obstacle: Physics (pressure, weight, fragility), nature (iron-eating bacteria, a hurricane), and morality.

beats.text: It's right there: we've sent cameras, subs, even tourists.
So why not raise it and charge admission?
Dozens of plans, all failed.
Obstacle 1: 2.5 miles down, 6,000 psi, and the 2023 sub implosion as proof.
Say you solve pressure: obstacle 2, 52,000 tons, no cable could lift it.
Obstacle 3: it's in two pieces and rotting; pull and it disintegrates.
So people got creative: ping-pong balls, petroleum jelly, ice, a novel's compressed air, each killed in a line.
Someone did raise part of it: 'the big piece'.
1996: crowds cheer as it surfaces, then a hurricane snaps the lines.
1998 retry succeeds, now on display in Las Vegas.
That took 4 years for 15 tons, against 52,000.
Meanwhile a unique bacterium is eating the ship; gone in 20-30 years.
The other reason: it's a grave (moment of silence, pairs of shoes on the seabed).
The UN and a treaty protect it like a cemetery.
Layered answer: we can't, and we shouldn't.
One face: a passenger's postcard to his mother.
The ocean is taking it back: a fitting end.

loops.q: What wild ideas did people try?
How did someone bring part of it up?
Will the big piece make it?

ending: A quiet moral reframe: maybe vanishing is the right end. Last image: a faint mark on the seafloor; time doing what time does.
facts: Q: why can't you just go down there? A: 6,000 psi, then the 2023 implosion shows what that does.
Q: why not lift it? A: 52,000 tons = 36,000 cars, and the one piece raised weighed 15.
jokes: ~1/min, mostly deadpan undercuts at the end of failed attempts ('and then a hurricane arrived', 'to put it mildly, not practical'). All on story beats.
template: [Famous thing] is right there; we've even [done lesser thing]. SO why hasn't anyone [obvious action]? It seems easy: [profit]. People tried and all failed. Obstacle 1 [physics] + a recent tragedy as proof. 'Say you solve that': obstacle 2 [scale + vivid comparison]. Obstacle 3 [it's not what you picture]. Wild-attempt montage, each killed in one line. BUT someone DID do a small piece: [mini-heist with crowd, setback, retry]. BUT scale: [tiny vs total]. Meanwhile [nature's clock erasing it]. AND the deeper reason: [moral]. Layered answer: can't AND shouldn't. One human face. Quiet final image.

title: What Happens After We Die?
want: (implicitly) to live, and to know what you experience
central_question: Your heart just stopped; what happens in the next 60 seconds, and is your brain at its most alive? (0:10)
stakes: Your life (the 4-6-minute reversible window) and what your final experience is.
obstacle: Time and biology (oxygen running out), plus science's limits.

beats.text: Your heart just stopped: second zero.
Claim: dying may be the most alive your brain ever is.
0 s: nothing you can feel; blood stops.
Your brain doesn't know yet: about 10 s of oxygen left, you're still you.
About 10 s: cortex shuts down, consciousness goes; from outside you look gone.
Inside, a 2023 study shows a gamma surge as the brain dies ('crazy high').
Pause: near-death reports match; life review is small moments, not highlights.
White-cat anecdote: a memory from 14 months old, confirmed by his mother.
Are all memories still in there? We don't know.
Meanwhile the body goes dark: 30 s, lactic acid, jaw drops, pupils fixed.
'Or are they?' Hospital studies: about 40% report some awareness, 3% full sight and sound.
Many report not being alone; the experience is mostly peaceful.
60 s: still reversible; self-digestion just beginning; limbo.
Waiting for what? Two answers: oxygen, or this was your last minute.
Your brain used that minute to turn on, not off.
Moral: survivors want time; the ordinary Tuesdays are what replays.

loops.q: What happens in the 60 s / most alive?
What does the life review really show?
Whose memory is the white cat?
Are all our memories still in there?

turns: 2:44 life review is trivia, not highlights
4:37 'or are they?' awareness reported while clinically dead
ending: A moral flip with a callback to the 'random Tuesday' (2:54): your brain recorded it all and may play it back. One loop (are all memories stored?) is deliberately left open.
facts: Q: what does the dying brain do? A: the 2023 gamma-surge study.
Q: is anyone 'in there' after the heart stops? A: hospital-study percentages for awareness.
jokes: Essentially none. Tension comes from the clock and from 'here's where it gets strange again' re-hooks.
template: [Clock event] just happened to you. Second zero. Claim: [counterintuitive]. Walk the clock: [t1 body fact] -> BUT [inside, the opposite] -> named study. Pause for [human reports] + one jaw-drop anecdote -> open question. Back to the body at [t2]. 'Or are they?' -> bigger study with percentages. [t3]: the reversible window. 'Waiting for what?' Two answers. Close: a moral + callback to the anecdote.

title: What Did Ancient Humans Do All Day?
protagonist: you, placed in a Hadza/Kung camp
want: (implicitly) the happiness and free time they seem to have
central_question: They work ~2.5 hours a day and look happier; so what do they actually do all day? (0:32)
stakes: What we traded away: time, closeness, equality.
obstacle: Our assumptions (hunters feed the camp, primitive = miserable) and modern life's bosses and bills.

beats.text: Right now a Hadza man is napping; his work day is done.
2.5 hours of work, fewer chronic diseases, more laughter; they look happier.
So what do they do all day? A 1968 time study: about 15 hours of work a week.
Walk the day with 'you' in it: sunrise, 25-30 people you've known forever.
First hour is talk, which is the camp's operating system and legal system.
An anthropologist's Christmas ox gets mocked for weeks, and the reason is equality.
Hunting is dramatic and usually fails.
The women feed the camp; grandmothers out-gather mothers.
Kids learn in mixed-age play groups: 'the school we evolved for'.
Midday: sharing is a rule, possibly what built our brains.
Afternoon: naps, lice, toilets, sex, all without shame.
Conflicts happen, and they end by walking away to another camp.
Late afternoon visits; hunters usually return empty.
This is not paradise: sickness, dead children.
Answer: the 'original affluent society' had time, not wealth.
We made real trades (vaccines) and hidden ones (bosses and bills).
We're still hunter-gatherers; we just stopped doing [their things]. (transcript cut)

loops.q: What do they do all day?
How do fights end without police?

turns: 3:43 the women, not the hunters, feed the camp
ending: Balanced ledger (real gains and hidden losses), with a callback to the opening's 'no boss, no rent' as 'bosses and bills', ending on the line that we are still them.
facts: Q: how much did they work? A: an anthropologist's minute-by-minute tally, about 15 h/week.
Q: who feeds the camp? A: women provide more than half the calories; grandmothers gather the most.
jokes: ~2/min (the funniest Zenn), mostly as tag lines at the end of each clock segment ('Most of us hit that before lunch', 'Generosity is the savings account'). They sit on story beats, and the ending stretch is joke-free.
template: Right now, somewhere, [person] is [enviable state]. [Stat vs you]. SO what do they actually do all day? Walk the clock with 'you' inside: Sunrise [scene] -> [surprising function] + one story with a twist -> Morning [the expected hero fails; the unexpected hero] -> Midday [a rule] -> Afternoon [taboo said flat] -> [how conflict ends] -> Evening. BUT this is not paradise. The answer: [abstract resource]. We made real trades AND hidden trades. Close: you still have their [body]; you just stopped [X].

title: The Slotow Effect
protagonist: rangers and ecologists at a South African reserve; the orphan elephants
want: stop the rhino killings without shooting their way out
central_question: Rhinos found dead with horns still on; who is killing them, and why? Framed as 'why the young need the old'. (0:00-0:45)
stakes: A rhino population nursed back from a few dozen animals; the orphans' lives.
obstacle: A wrong theory (trauma, bad elephants) and a missing piece nobody could supply (adult bulls couldn't be moved).

beats.text: 1994: dead rhinos, and poachers are the obvious suspect.
The horn is still attached.
Wounds from above, elephant-sized prints.
Elephants don't kill rhinos; this one was hunting.
Rewind to 1979: a new park is stocked with 18 orphan calves and no adults.
Why orphans? Culls shot the matriarch first, then the herd; only calves could be trucked.
Nobody was a villain; the orphans were left to raise themselves.
They turn nervous and aggressive, and two adult females can't fix it.
Charges, a tourist killed, the hunter sent to stop it killed too.
1994: 20 rhinos dead in a year.
Rangers work it like a serial case and shoot three suspects; the killings stop.
1996: 20 more die. Wrong elephants.
Two-year surveillance, rap sheets, a suspect named 'Tom Thumb', a 1997 catch in the act.
Trauma explains anger but not timing; the clusters have a rhythm.
Every killer was a young male in musth, which normally starts late and short.
Older bulls switch musth off just by existing, and this park had none.
Diagnosis flips: the park didn't have bad elephants, it was missing elephants.
Import adult bulls (newly possible with new trucks).
Outranked, the young bulls' musth collapses; the killings stop completely.
Callback: even Tom Thumb left the rhinos alone; paper in Nature.
Lesson: a society has an architecture; humans will never get this experiment.

ending: Extrapolates the lesson to human neighbourhoods we can never experiment on; final line (transcript cut) says nothing about them changed except their surroundings.
facts: Q: why no adults? A: the cull method (matriarch first; calves the only ones small enough to truck).
Q: why the killing clusters? A: the musth mechanism and how older bulls cap it.
jokes: ~0.5/min, deadpan ('mostly by ignoring each other') and one callback (Tom Thumb). All on story beats.
template: [Year]: [victims] found dead. Obvious suspect [X], BUT [clue rules X out]. Clues point to [impossible culprit], BUT [culprit] never does this. SO rewind: how [culprit] got here, a well-meant decision with a dark detail; nobody was a villain. Warning signs -> escalation -> body count. Investigators act on [wrong theory]; it works, BUT it happens again. Surveillance, a named suspect. Two theories: [obvious] vs [precise]; the timing reveals [mechanism], and what normally switches it off is [missing element]. Diagnosis flip: not bad [X], missing [Y]. Fix: put [Y] back, and it stops in a season. Callback to the named suspect. Lesson for humans.

title: The Spotlight Effect
central_question: Is everyone really watching you? (answered almost at once: no, 0:10). The working question is why it feels that way. (2:12)
stakes: Every hand you didn't raise and every thing you didn't try.
obstacle: Your own brain's ancient software (anchoring, tribe-era fear).

beats.text: You walk in late; everyone sees the stain and the sweat.
What really happened: two glances, nobody cared.
It has a name: the spotlight effect.
The embarrassing-T-shirt study: wearers guess 50% noticed; under 25% did.
Variations: flattering shirts, group discussions, same result.
Why? Anchoring on your own vivid experience.
The elevator example: you're the star, they're scenery.
Roots: in a tribe of 150, reputation meant survival.
You live among 8 billion, and your brain hasn't caught up.
Its cousin: the illusion of transparency (speeches, bitter drinks).
Just knowing about it made speakers perform better.
Counterpoint, social media: it still holds.
What it cost you: every hand not raised.
You're free: go to the restaurant alone, wear the shirt.
Inverted callback: they're worried about who's looking at them.

loops.q: Does it hold up in tests?
Why does your brain do this?

ending: Empowerment list, then the opening room scene inverted: everyone is busy worrying about themselves.
facts: Q: how visible are you really? A: guessed 50% vs actual under 25% in the T-shirt study.
Q: can knowing help? A: the follow-up study where informed speakers were rated more composed.
jokes: ~0.8/min; small relatable tags. Note it's the lowest-viewed Zenn and the one with the weakest open loop.
template: You [embarrassing scene]; everyone saw. BUT what actually happened: [deflation]. It has a name. Classic experiment: [guess vs reality %]. Variations. WHY: [mechanism] + everyday example. Evolutionary root -> mismatch with now. A deeper cousin effect. Payoff: knowing helps. A counterpoint answered. The life cost list. Close: invert the opening scene.

title: Why Humans Eat 3 Meals a Day
want: to know whether three meals is natural
central_question: Nobody decided 3 meals from biology; it's 'a story'. Where did it come from? (0:20; restated 3:23)
stakes: Low/personal: whether your routine is biology or habit (and eating late is worse).
obstacle: A wrong belief (it's natural) plus cultural bias and commerce.

beats.text: You ate breakfast, lunch, dinner and never questioned it.
No biology decided it: three meals is a story.
23,000 years ago at a lakeside camp: people ate whenever.
Agriculture brings reliable food.
Still no three meals: Egypt ate two.
Greeks ate three-ish, loosely.
The super-organized Romans feared more than one meal as gluttony.
European settlers called Native fasting 'uncivilized', and that bias later spread three meals.
Where exactly from? The Royal Navy's ship routine.
What locked it in: factory clocks; 'not a discovery, a solution'.
Breakfast vs mass; dinner migrates to evening with lamps.
A cereal entrepreneur sells breakfast as most important: commerce, not science.
Does biology want it? Circadian timing matters more than count.
Biology isn't everything: shared meals bond us.
Recap as a 'because...because...' chain.
Tonight you'll sit for dinner, and now you'll know why.

loops.q: Where did the 3-meal story come from?
Did organized Rome have a schedule?

turns: 0:10 it's not biology, it's a story
ending: Callback to the opening ('tonight you'll sit for dinner') with closure: now you know why. Calm, no sting.
facts: Q: did the Romans eat 3 meals? A: a food historian on Roman fear of gluttony and one main meal.
Q: why does breakfast matter so much today? A: cereal marketing in the 1920s-30s.
jokes: Near zero. Interest comes from 'you might expect X; they did not' reversals.
template: You [daily habit] and never questioned it. BUT nobody decided it from [biology]; it's a story. Go back [N] years: [no habit]. [Big change] still didn't create it. Culture A did [variant], culture B [variant], the culture you'd expect to invent it [rejected it]. SO where exactly did it come from? [Institution] -> [industrial force] locked it; 'not a discovery, a solution'. AND [commerce] cemented it. BUT does your body want it? [Science: what actually matters]. BUT [human/social layer]. Recap as a because-chain. Close: next time you [habit], you'll know why.

title: The Rarest Human Possible
protagonist: a dream woman (later revealed to be the 'rarest human'), and you the dreamer
want: you want to know if she could exist
central_question: Does a person like her exist? Then: what would the rarest possible human look like? (0:35-0:38)
stakes: Light: the romance/fantasy, then your own uniqueness.

beats.text: You meet a striking woman in a park and fall in love.
The alarm rings; it was a dream.
Does she exist? Yes; bigger question: what is the rarest possible person?
Trait 1: a tiny ethnic group gives 1 in 16 million.
Albinism: 1 in 320 billion.
Complete heterochromia.
Left-handed: 1 in 5.33 quadrillion.
Tetrachromacy.
Hyperthymesia.
Recap the build: it's the woman from the dream.
1 in 6.83 septillion, more than the stars in the universe.
And this isn't even the rarest possible.
